Any guidance would be much appreciated. Apologies for my R ignorance!

Many thanks,

Gemma

Rather than answer your questions 1 and 2; I'll stop you at the point where you say

"Since each row in the flatfile represents a detection I figure I cannot include effort and samples where there were no detections in this table."

That is not an accurate statement, it is very common for there to be transects without detections, so there must be some way to accommodate that in the data files.  The answer lies by looking at an example data file associated with the Distance R package

http://distancesampling.org/R/vignettes/minke.csv

If you examine that comma-delimited text file, you will see that transect 5 in the South stratum as well as transect 6 in that stratum had no detections (lines 26 and 27 in the file).  The way to determine this is to note that those rows contain stratum name, stratum size, transect label, transect length, *but no distance*.  There is a comma after transect length but no value following the comma.

That is the way in which you construct a 'flatfile' for surveys that include transects with no sightings. If you are happy with the 'flatfile' format, then I will not answer your questions about region/sample/obs tables.  See if that works for you.

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Response distribution family
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Response distribution family
messages.body_plain:
Hi Paula, hi listfolk,

The two metrics that you describe are measuring two different properties
of the model. The check plots (particularly the Q-Q plot) measures the
degree to which the assumptions of the model are violated (e.g. are the
residuals of the model normally distributed, in the case of the Q-Q
plot), whereas the R^2 value is telling you something about the
closeness of the model to the observed data.

Indeed, one could have a very high R^2 value for a model that violates
its assumptions -- making inference (e.g. variance estimates) from the
model highly unreliable despite the apparently "good" R^2.

[There are a number of other reasons to be wary of R^2 even in simple
linear models (see e.g.
http://www.stat.cmu.edu/~cshalizi/mreg/15/lectures/10/lecture-10.pdf),
so I generally don't view R^2 as a necessarily good way of thinking
about how "good" our models are.]

On that topic, I don't think any single metric makes sense to select
between spatial models (and probably no single model truly describes
what's going on), but for practical purposes I'd recommend ensuring that
the model meets its assumptions first (gam.check(), ensuring smooth
terms are sufficiently wiggly, checking for heteroskedasticity, etc),
then think about how well the model describes the data (things like R^2
or deviance explained, AIC etc).

Perhaps others on this list have different opinions on this?

Hope this helps,
--dave

messages.body_plain:
Dear List,

Rob Williams asked about using additional ("transit-leg") sightings in the detection function, but not density estimation.

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/distance-sampling/_PgfTxiSTO0

Here, I would like to extend the question, as to whether one may use these sightings to estimate density.

My aim is to use model-based distance sampling methods to estimate the abundance and spatial distribution of pack-ice seals (e.g., density-surface models - Hedley et al. 2004).

Part of the dataset comprises a digital strip-transect survey (images, providing continuous cover of the transect, taken from fixed wing aircraft). The survey design comprised (only) 11 parallel transects (~ north / south orientation) with 37 km “transit legs” connecting each transect (i.e., a regular, systematic design).

The study area is not bounded by a coastline or (at the time) the ice / open water edge. Therefore, I do not expect edge effects, or a density gradient relative to transects, or transit legs.

Following the flight, seals were counted on images corresponding to both transects and ‘transit legs’. Should I restrict density surface modelling to transect data, or can I also use observations from transit legs (and equivalently, in-bound and out-bound legs)?

Any feedback will be appreciated

If anyone reads this post prior to surveying, they may do well to refer to Buckland et al (2004) Chapter 7 for alternative survey designs to minimize ‘off-effort’ time.

Chris

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Using additional (transit-leg) sightings for model-based inference / DSM
messages.body_plain:
Chris

The sensitivity regarding differentiation of on- and off-effort sightings that arise in the earlier correspondence by Dr. Williams is relevant when a design-based inference is drawn from a survey.  When using model-based inference, the sensitivity is placed elsewhere.

Design-based inference assumes the locations where survey effort is applied are representative of where effort is not placed.  This is usually accomplished by random systematic sampling.  That is the mechanism that permits the "inferential leap" from where you collected data to where you did not collect data.

With model-based inference, the mechanism permitting the inferential leap is different.  Model-based inference assumes the modelled relationship between environmental covariates and encounters is the same in the areas that did not receive effort as areas that did receive effort.  Hence "design" of surveys to receive model-based analysis should emphasis "representativeness of the environmental covariate space".  Therefore, it is fine to use sightings from the transit and in/outbound legs in your model-based analysis; assuming the relationship between seal sightings and environmental covariates on those legs is equivalent to the relationship in the rest of the study area.

Hope that's useful.

Any advice welcome,

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] combine stratum level density estimates outside distance
messages.body_plain:
Christian

It should be possible to perform your higher level estimation by hand (with the help of R) in the case of strata being geographic.  Essentially, the density at the "higher level" is the average of the component densities.  However this average is a weighted average, most commonly weighted by the areas of the component strata.

The other component of this re-aggregation is whether there are dependencies between components.  Dependencies have consequences for the calculation of variance, hence confidence intervals. If the component estimates are all estimated independently, calculations are easy.  Calculations are made mildly more complicated if, for example, a common detection function was used for multiple strata, hence there is an induced dependency between strata.

Section 3.7.1 of Buckland et al. (2001) provides a set of formulae for coping with variance calculations in the face of dependency.  Have a look there and get back to us if the information in the text does not cover your situation.

messages.subject_clean: using additional ("transit-leg") sightings in the detection function, but not in estimating density
messages.body_plain:
Hi Rob,

Thanks for the question, and to Stewart for his answer.  Stewart is right, but it's also possible to do it using the CDS or MCDS engine - and this is probably easier for single platform data.

As you suggested, the trick is to set up a separate stratum for your off-effort sightings.  The key thing is to set the area to zero.  Line length is not allowed to be zero, but so long as you use a positive value it doesn't matter what you set that to.  Then, set up an analysis where you estimate the detection function globally (i.e., pooling both the off effort stratum and any other strata you have) and density by stratum as well as globally.  (To do this, in Model Definition, Estimate tab, tick "User layer type Stratum" and under Quantities to estimate, tick Density Global and Stratum, and Detection function Global.(If you're using the MCDS engine, rather than CDS, you would tick Detection function Global and Stratum) )  Set the Global density estimate to be the mean of the stratum-level estimates, weighted by Area (this is the default in the Estimate tab.)

When you run the model, you'll get a warning that the Area=0 for your off-effort stratum, but you can ignore that.  Distance will use all the detections for fitting the detection function, which is what you want.  It will give you a nonsense encounter rate and density estimate for the off-effort stratum, but you don't care about that -- you only care about your on-effort stratum.  If you have more than one on-effort stratum (i.e., a stratified survey) the global density estimate is correct (i.e., ignores the off-effort stratum) because you set the area to zero. The global density is a weighted average of the stratum-level estimates with the weight being the area, and so the weight for this stratum is zero.

Hope this helps.  I couldn't find this tip in the manual, so it's been helpful that you've asked and so we can document the answer in this group.

Cheers, Len

messages.subject: Multi-species Sampling & Sufficient Sample Size
messages.subject_clean: Multi-species Sampling & Sufficient Sample Size
messages.body_plain:
Greetings DISTANCE users,

I am trying to quantify the effect of various timber harvest regimes on nesting guilds in bottomland forests using a BACI design. I want to generate accurate species densities derived from 4 years of avian point count surveys but fear my sample sizes are too small to use program DISTANCE.

A little background:

I have 3 sites. Each site is divided into 3 experimental forest stands (= 9 EFS; ~24 ha each). Each EFS was randomly assigned 1 of 3 treatments (moderate, intense, no-harvest control). Thus, I have 3 replicates of each treatment. Birds were surveyed in 2010 and 2012 (before harvest) then again in 2014 and 2015 (after harvest). Individuals were placed into 10-m distance intervals (heaped). The 40 point count stations are distributed evenly across the 3 sites (4-5 per EFS). Each point was visited 2 times each breeding season (May and June).

Naturally, some species were detected more frequently than others due to louder song, commonness, etc. However, I am unclear as to whether even the most common species' sample sizes can be considered adequate to fit a detection function and if I can obtain reliable density estimates using program DISTANCE.

As I understand it, minimum sample size should be no less than 40 detections per stratum (per visit, too?) so as to fit a detection function. If so, even the most common species do not have enough detections after 2 visits.

E.g. Carolina Chickadee: total detections (within 100 m) across all experimental forest stands and 2 visits (May and June) = 54.

At first this seemed like a reasonable number of detections, but sample size is still <40 individuals per stratum (EFS). When I run the CDS engine in program DISTANCE, transform data into intervals (10), and use "stratum" as layer type, I obtain many warnings stating that I have a limited number of observations. DISTANCE still provides density estimates but I assume these can not be trusted.

If indeed my samples are too small, is there another option? Could I group species into nesting guilds and then obtain density estimates? I assume no because of differences in detectability...

I am reading Buckland et al. 2001 Introduction to Distance Sampling and the DISTANCE user manual, but I can not seem to find a straight answer regarding sample size.

If anyone could offer some clarification I would appreciate it.

Thank you,

Jennifer

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Degrees of freedom from chi-square GOF
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Degrees of freedom from chi-square GOF
messages.body_plain:
Kristen

Thanks for your thorough description of your analysis.  As is often the case, I'll suggest a different approach to your analysis that circumvents your specific degrees of freedom question, but I'll return to the degrees of freedom question at the end of this message.

The detections in the field, I presume were measured exactly (otherwise you would be unlikely to re-adjust your bin widths between 3 and 8).  If the distance measures are exact, then I suggest you use the goodness of fit measures derived from the QQ plots produced by Distance, namely the Kolomogorov-Smirnov or Cramer von Mises tests.  Using exact distances to assess fit avoids the subjective aspect of selecting the 'proper' number of bins and locations of cutpoints.  The only reason to convert exact distances to grouped distances is if there is a problem in the data collection/recording caused by rounding.

Back to your challenge with deducing degrees of freedom for repeated analyses with varying numbers of bins.  For binned (or grouped) data, the degrees of freedom of the chi-square test is defined as u-q-1, where u is the number of bins and q is the number of parameters in the detection function.  The tricky part is the number of parameters in the detection function when using adjustment terms.  You noted the use of cosine, simple and Hermite polynomial adjustments in your fitting.  The number of parameters in the detection function will depend not only upon the number of parameters in the key function (0 for uniform, 1 for half normal and 2 for hazard rate) but also upon the number of adjustment terms used.  The number of adjustment terms is chosen by the Distance software so you will need to read the model output closely to determine the number of adjustment terms associated with the chosen model.  Moving the cutpoints will change the shape of the histogram of detections, resulting in differing numbers of adjustment terms being selected.

Section 5.1.4 of Buckland et al. (2015) discusses the topic of goodness of fit in more detail.
Buckland, S., E. Rexstad, T. Marques and C. Oedekoven. 2015. Distance Sampling: Methods and Applications. Springer.

messages.body_plain:
Jennifer

Thanks for the detailed explanation of your study design.  Questions about sample size are very common on this list.  Sample sizes come in two flavours: one dealing with fitting of detection functions and the other dealing with design-based inference (from locations sampled near points to areas outside point cover).  You express concern about the former, but the latter is also of interest.  It seems that you wish to have density estimates at the experimental forest stand level, with 4-5 points per stand.  That is likely to make your estimates of variability between points within stand potentially troublesome because 10-20 replicates per stand is preferable.

However, back to the question you posted about detection function sample size.  Section 2.4.1 of Buckland et al. (2015) discusses sample size in the context of detection function modelling, recognising sample sizes are guidelines rather than absolutes.  This book section also points out that employing covariates, perhaps species and site in your situation, may assist in doing an adequate job of fitting a detection function to your data.

When you conquer various sample size and detection function issues and you arrive at your stand-level density estimates, the next question is what to do with those estimates to address your question of the consequence of harvest regimes upon bird density.  The likelihood is you will take some sort of ANOVA route; however, the question then becomes how to incorporate the uncertainty in each of your stand-level estimates.  Read on...

Buckland et al. (2015) Sections 3.2.5 and 7.4.1 also describes a study of the effects of forestry practices (in this case prescribed burns) upon bird density.  The nature of the analysis of the prescribed burn study places the analysis of the distance sampling data into a more general analysis framework, based upon previous work published in Buckland et al. (2009).  You may wish to read those references for a broad context of the multiple stages of analysis ahead.
Buckland, S., E. Rexstad, T. Marques and C. Oedekoven. 2015. Distance Sampling: Methods and Applications. Springer.
Buckland, S., R. Russell, B. Dickson, V. Saab, D. Gorman and W. Block. 2009. Analysing designed experiments in distance sampling. J. Agr. Biol. Ecol. Stats. 14:432-442.

On Monday, May 23, 2016 at 4:48:41 AM UTC-5, Eric Rexstad wrote:
>
> Kristen
>
> Thanks for your thorough description of your analysis.  As is often the case, I'll suggest a different approach to your analysis that circumvents your specific degrees of freedom question, but I'll return to the degrees of freedom question at the end of this message.
>
> The detections in the field, I presume were measured exactly (otherwise you would be unlikely to re-adjust your bin widths between 3 and 8).  If the distance measures are exact, then I suggest you use the goodness of fit measures derived from the QQ plots produced by Distance, namely the Kolomogorov-Smirnov or Cramer von Mises tests.  Using exact distances to assess fit avoids the subjective aspect of selecting the 'proper' number of bins and locations of cutpoints.  The only reason to convert exact distances to grouped distances is if there is a problem in the data collection/recording caused by rounding.
>
> Back to your challenge with deducing degrees of freedom for repeated analyses with varying numbers of bins.  For binned (or grouped) data, the degrees of freedom of the chi-square test is defined as u-q-1, where u is the number of bins and q is the number of parameters in the detection function.  The tricky part is the number of parameters in the detection function when using adjustment terms.  You noted the use of cosine, simple and Hermite polynomial adjustments in your fitting.  The number of parameters in the detection function will depend not only upon the number of parameters in the key function (0 for uniform, 1 for half normal and 2 for hazard rate) but also upon the number of adjustment terms used.  The number of adjustment terms is chosen by the Distance software so you will need to read the model output closely to determine the number of adjustment terms associated with the chosen model.  Moving the cutpoints will change the shape of the histogram of detections, resulting in differing numbers of adjustment terms being selected.
>
> Section 5.1.4 of Buckland et al. (2015) discusses the topic of goodness of fit in more detail.
> Buckland, S., E. Rexstad, T. Marques and C. Oedekoven. 2015. Distance Sampling: Methods and Applications. Springer.
